passage: The power had gone out in the village again, so the whole lane sat on Dadaji's charpai under the neem tree. Anand, nine, held the lantern. Sunaina, his cousin, kept poking him to stop swinging it. Dadaji told them about the old stepwell behind the temple, how the king's daughter had it dug during a drought so no one had to walk to the river. "She sold her own bangles to pay the workers," he said. Anand frowned. "Then why is it named after the king?" Dadaji laughed. "Good question. Stories remember some people louder than others." The next morning Anand and Sunaina went to the stepwell and counted the steps. Sunaina found a small carved bangle on the third pillar.

qa.q: Where did the family sit when the power went out?
qa.a: They sat on Dadaji's charpai under the neem tree in the lane.

qa.q: Why did Anand frown when he heard the story?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair that the king got the name when his daughter had sold her bangles to build the stepwell; he was noticing whose part the story leaves out.

qa.q: How could Dadaji keep Anand's curiosity about local history going?
qa.a: He could take the children to the stepwell or to older neighbours so they can collect more versions of the story and compare them.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunaina to find the carved bangle on the pillar?
qa.a: It probably makes the story feel real to her, as if the daughter's part is written into the stone even if the name is not.

grounding: It shows a child hearing a local legend from a grandparent, questioning its lesson and linking it to a real place in the village.

passage: Every Friday in Mr Okafor's flat in Leeds, Chidi's grandfather told one tale about Tortoise, the clever, greedy trickster from home. Gabriel, Chidi's best mate from the flat upstairs, had started coming down just for this. Tonight Tortoise tricked the birds into lending him feathers, then ate the whole feast himself. The birds took their feathers back, and Tortoise fell and cracked his shell. "That's why his shell has patches," said Grandpa. Gabriel grinned. "My nan tells one where the fox steals the cheese from a crow. Same thing, really. Greedy one loses." Chidi looked pleased and a little proud. "Next Friday you tell yours," he said. "Then Grandpa can check if it's the same lesson."

qa.q: What did Tortoise do with the feast in Grandpa's story?
qa.a: He ate the whole feast himself after borrowing feathers from the birds.

qa.q: What does Chidi's pleased, proud look suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems glad that his friend enjoys his family's stories and sees them as worth comparing, which makes his heritage feel valued.

qa.q: How could Grandpa build on Gabriel's idea of swapping stories?
qa.a: He could let each boy tell a tale and then ask them together what the two stories are trying to teach and how they differ.

qa.q: How might Gabriel see the Friday stories now?
qa.a: He probably sees them as a fun ritual he belongs to, and a way to notice that his nan's stories share lessons with Chidi's family's tales.

grounding: It shows children learning a folk tale and its moral from a grandparent and linking it to a story from another tradition.

passage: The Class 5 trip to the district museum started badly. Rashmi's group got the dusty room with the old coins and a broken plough. "This is boring," Bhavna whispered. Then the guide, a retired schoolteacher, picked up a clay lamp. "Two hundred years ago, the people of your town lit this during the salt march meeting in the market square," she said. "Your market. The one near the sweet shop." Rashmi's eyes widened. She had bought jalebi there on Sunday. Bhavna leaned in. By the end, the two girls had filled a whole page of notes and argued about which street the crowd had walked down. On the bus home, Rashmi pressed her face to the window as they passed the square.

qa.q: What object did the guide pick up in the museum room?
qa.a: She picked up a clay lamp.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi's eyes widen when the guide mentioned the market?
qa.a: She suddenly realised the history happened in a place she knows, near the sweet shop where she bought jalebi on Sunday, so it felt personal and exciting.

qa.q: What could a teacher learn from how the guide changed the girls' mood?
qa.a: Linking old objects to places children already know turns dull facts into their own story, so starting from the town's streets could help other lessons too.

qa.q: What would change if the guide had only read out dates from a label?
qa.a: Bhavna might have stayed bored, and the girls would not have argued over the route or looked at the square differently on the way home.

grounding: It shows children in a school museum visit connecting their region's history to familiar streets.

passage: My sister Disha is ten and very serious about rules, so I was surprised last week. Her friend Rekha invited her home for Christmas Eve, and Disha came back talking nonstop. She told me Rekha's family sang songs in the evening and put a small star on top of the tree. She had asked Rekha's mother why they made a little crib with animals, and listened to the whole answer. At dinner, Mummy asked if she ate the cake. "Only after I asked if it had egg," Disha said. "Aunty didn't mind. She made me a plain one." Then Disha tied a paper star to our window. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she hummed while she did it. 🙂

qa.q: What did Disha tie to the window after the visit?
qa.a: She tied a paper star to the family's window.

qa.q: What does Disha's nonstop talk and humming suggest she felt about Rekha's festival?
qa.a: She came back talking nonstop, listened to the full answer about the crib, and hummed while hanging a paper star, which suggests curiosity and admiration.

qa.q: What was respectful about how Disha handled the cake?
qa.a: She asked politely about egg instead of refusing or eating it without thinking, which respected both her own family's food habits and her host's effort.

qa.q: How might Rekha's mother see Disha after the evening?
qa.a: She probably saw a curious, polite guest who took an interest in their customs, and was happy to make a plain cake so Disha could join in.

grounding: It shows, through a sibling's eyes, a child learning about a friend's faith festival and respecting it while keeping her own practices.

passage:
Monday: Rukmini told the class that her neighbours were fasting through the day for Ramzan and she sometimes joined their evening meal, and Rashmi snorted, "No lunch for a month? That's silly." Rukmini went quiet. Rashmi saw her face and felt a bit bad, but didn't say anything.

Thursday: Rashmi asked her mother about it. Amma explained that Rashmi's Nani also fasted on some days, in her own way, and that it meant something to her. Rashmi thought about that a long time.

The next Tuesday: Rukmini brought dates that her neighbour had sent for the evening meal. Rashmi took one, said, "Thank you, and sorry about Monday," and asked what they ate first when the fast ended.

qa.q: What did Rukmini bring to school on the next Tuesday?
qa.a: She brought dates her neighbour had sent for the evening meal.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she saw Rukmini go quiet on Monday?
qa.a: She felt a bit bad because she realised her snort had hurt Rukmini, though she wasn't ready to say so yet.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi change her attitude, and what could she try next?
qa.a: Linking the fast to her own Nani's fasting helped her see its meaning; next time she could ask a question first instead of laughing.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini when Rashmi apologises and asks about the meal?
qa.a: It probably feels like relief and being taken seriously, since the practice she shared is now treated with interest instead of mockery.

grounding: It shows a child moving over several days from mocking a different faith practice to asking about it respectfully.

passage: Sit, Swati, I'll tell you about Manjula, my best friend when I was your age. Our lane had a small gurdwara at one end. Every Sunday we could smell the dal from the langar kitchen. Manjula was curious, but her father said, "That's their place, not ours." One day she walked in with her head uncovered, and a lady gently handed her a scarf. Manjula went red. The lady just smiled and showed her where to wash her hands. After that, Manjula helped roll rotis there every week, and she still lit her diya at home every evening. When I asked if she had changed religions, she laughed. "No, silly. I just learned their rules so I don't hurt anyone."

qa.q: What did the lady hand Manjula when she walked in?
qa.a: She gently handed her a scarf to cover her head.

qa.q: Why did Manjula go red when the lady handed her the scarf?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed because she realised she had broken a custom of the place without knowing, and she worried she might have been disrespectful.

qa.q: What could Swati take from Manjula's story if she visits another faith's place?
qa.a: She could ask or watch for the customs, like covering her head or washing hands, and follow them while still keeping her own practices at home.

qa.q: How might Manjula's father have seen her weekly visits?
qa.a: He may have worried at first that she was crossing a line, but he might see over time that she kept her own diya and simply learned to respect her neighbours.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood friend learning the customs of another faith's place of worship and respecting them while keeping her own.

passage: Diego's family in Valencia says one short thank-you before dinner, all holding hands. Diego, ten, usually rushes it so he can eat. Tonight his friend Emeka was staying over. Emeka's family says theirs silently, eyes closed. When Diego's father said, "Shall we?", Emeka looked unsure. Diego's mother smiled. "You can say yours your way, love." So Emeka bowed his head quietly while the others spoke. Diego peeked at him. Emeka looked so calm that Diego slowed down for once and actually thought about the words. After the meal, he asked Emeka what he thought about during the quiet. "Mostly my mum's cooking," Emeka said. "And today, your mum."

qa.q: How does Diego's family say thank-you before dinner?
qa.a: They say one short thank-you together while holding hands.

qa.q: Why did Diego slow down during the thank-you tonight?
qa.a: Watching how calm Emeka looked in his quiet prayer made Diego curious and made him want to mean the words instead of rushing them.

qa.q: How did Diego's mother help Emeka feel included?
qa.a: She invited him to give thanks in his own way, so he could join the moment without having to copy a practice that was not his family's.

qa.q: How might Emeka feel about the evening?
qa.a: He likely felt welcome and grateful, since his quiet habit was respected and he even included Diego's mum in his thanks. 🙂

grounding: It shows children taking part in a short family gratitude ritual and noticing what reflection feels like.

passage: The hostel warden at the boys' school rang a small bell at six each evening. For two minutes, everyone in the study hall sat still. Noor, eleven and new, hated it at first. His leg jiggled. He peeked at the clock. Zubin, the older boy beside him, kept his eyes closed and his hands loose on the desk. On the fourth evening, Noor tried it too. He heard the fan, a crow outside, someone's stomach growling. He nearly laughed. Then he thought of his mother's voice on the phone the night before, and his chest felt warm and tight at once. When the bell rang again, Zubin nudged him. "Better?" Noor shrugged, but he didn't reach for his pen straight away.

qa.q: How long did the evening silence in the study hall last?
qa.a: It lasted two minutes, starting and ending with a small bell.

qa.q: What does Noor's warm and tight chest suggest when he thinks of his mother?
qa.a: It suggests he misses home and is grateful for her at the same time; the quiet gave space for feelings he had been pushing aside.

qa.q: How could the warden help new boys like Noor settle into the silence?
qa.a: He could tell them it is fine to fidget at first and suggest one simple thing to notice, like sounds or someone they are thankful for.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Noor's shrug at the end?
qa.a: He might read it as a quiet yes, since Noor didn't grab his pen right away, and feel glad the new boy is settling in.

grounding: It shows a boy slowly joining a short daily silence practice at a hostel and finding a moment of reflection.

passage: I'm Kamal, and my little brother Yogesh is eight. Our Nani lights the lamp every morning and says a short prayer. Yogesh used to run past, looking for his socks. This month something changed. I saw him stop at the doorway, fold his hands and stand still while Nani sang. He doesn't know all the words, so he moves his lips a bit late. Yesterday he put a marigold near the lamp, one he had picked from the neighbour's pot, which Nani pretended not to notice. At night he whispers to himself before sleeping. I asked him once what he says. He said, "Just thank you. For today." I can't tell if he means it the way Nani does, but he seems calmer.

qa.q: What did Yogesh put near the lamp yesterday?
qa.a: He put a marigold he had picked from the neighbour's pot.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's whispering at night suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he has started his own small gratitude habit, thanking the day in his own words, which may make him feel calm.

qa.q: How could Nani gently support Yogesh's new habit?
qa.a: She could teach him one or two lines of the prayer slowly, or invite him to light the lamp with her, without making him feel tested.

qa.q: Why might Kamal be unsure about what the prayer means to Yogesh?
qa.a: Kamal only sees the outside, the folded hands and whispers, so he can guess Yogesh is calmer but cannot know what he feels inside.

grounding: An older sibling observes a younger child beginning to join a family prayer and a simple gratitude habit.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Monday was chess club: I lost twice and yawned. Tuesday was dance with Usha, which was fun but my feet got tangled. Today Masi gave me an old camera with no film, only a screen. I took 43 photos of ants carrying a crumb across the balcony. I forgot to eat my snack! Usha called and I missed it 😅. When I looked at the clock, a whole hour was gone and I didn't even notice. Mummy said, "You were so still, Hansa, I thought you were asleep." I'm not sure if I want to be a photographer or an ant scientist. Maybe both? Tomorrow I'm going to try the camera on the pigeons.

qa.q: How many photos did Hansa take of the ants?
qa.a: She took 43 photos of ants carrying a crumb across the balcony.

qa.q: What does losing a whole hour suggest Hansa felt about the camera compared with chess or dance?
qa.a: She forgot her snack, missed Usha's call and lost track of a whole hour, while in chess she just yawned.

qa.q: How could Hansa's mother support this new interest?
qa.a: She could let Hansa keep experimenting with the camera and ask her to show her favourite photos, without pushing her to choose a career yet.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about the missed call?
qa.a: She may feel a little ignored at first, but if Hansa explains and shares her ant photos, Usha may find it funny and interesting.

grounding: It shows a child trying several activities and noticing which one makes her lose track of time.

passage: In the kasba, Salma's father runs a small cycle-repair shop beside the bus stand. Chandrika, Salma's friend from Class 6, started coming after school to wait for her bus. At first she only sat on the tyre pile, bored. Then one day a boy's chain slipped, and Salma's father was busy. Chandrika picked up a spanner. "Show me?" Salma laughed, but her father nodded. Chandrika watched how he hooked the chain back, then did the next one herself, grease up to her wrists. After that she missed two buses in a week. At home her mother scolded her for her black nails. Chandrika only said, "Amma, I want to learn how the gears work."

qa.q: Where is Salma's father's shop?
qa.a: It is beside the bus stand in the kasba.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika miss two buses in a week?
qa.a: She was so absorbed in fixing the cycles that she lost track of time; the repair work had caught her interest in a way sitting on the tyre pile never did.

qa.q: How could Chandrika's mother respond to this new interest?
qa.a: Instead of only scolding about her nails, she could ask what she is learning and help her plan her time so she doesn't miss the bus.

qa.q: How does Salma's father seem to see Chandrika's interest?
qa.a: He takes it seriously, nodding and letting her try, which suggests he respects her wish to learn even though she is a young girl in his shop.

grounding: It shows a child discovering an absorbing hobby through trying a new activity in a small town.

passage: Tariq's mum signed him up for a Saturday taster day at the community centre in Rotterdam. Four stations, twenty minutes each. At football, Tariq kept glancing at the clock. At drawing, he sketched one lopsided boat and stopped. At cooking, he and Alejandro, a boy he'd just met, burned the pancakes and laughed. The last station was a small electronics table with buzzers and wires. Tariq made a bulb light up, then made it blink. The leader called time, and Tariq didn't hear her. Alejandro had to tap his shoulder. On the tram home, Tariq kept drawing circuits on the steamed-up window. "Can I go back next week?" he asked. "Just to the wires."

qa.q: What did Tariq and Alejandro burn at the cooking station?
qa.a: They burned the pancakes.

qa.q: What does Tariq not hearing the leader call time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was completely absorbed by the electronics, far more than by the other stations where he watched the clock.

qa.q: What small step could Tariq's mum take to support this interest?
qa.a: She could find a regular beginner electronics group or simple kit so he can keep exploring it, while still letting him try other things.

qa.q: How might Alejandro remember the taster day differently from Tariq?
qa.a: For Alejandro the fun part may have been the burned pancakes and meeting Tariq, since each child finds different activities absorbing.

grounding: It shows a child trying many short activities and noticing which one holds his attention.

passage: The school's eco club met every Wednesday in the science lab. This week, Mahima, a Class 6 girl, brought a surprising chart. She had checked every tap in the girls' washroom for a week. "Three drip all day," she said. "I held a bottle under one. It filled in one lunch break." Arnab, who ran the club, whistled. Their teacher asked what they could do. Mahima had a list ready: write to the caretaker, put little signs above the sinks, and switch off the corridor fans at break. Arnab added, "And we check again next month." Two weeks later, the caretaker fixed the taps. Mahima drew a small smiling tap on the sign 🙂.

qa.q: How many taps in the girls' washroom dripped all day?
qa.a: Three taps dripped all day.

qa.q: What does Mahima's list suggest about how she felt about the dripping taps?
qa.a: It suggests she was bothered by the waste and determined to fix it, since she tested it for a week and came with ready steps.

qa.q: Why was Arnab's idea to check again next month useful?
qa.a: It turns one action into a habit and lets the club see whether the changes, like signs and switching off fans, actually keep working.

qa.q: How might the caretaker see the children's letter?
qa.a: He might be glad someone noticed and reported the problem clearly, or at first feel it was more work, but the fixed taps show he took it seriously.

grounding: It shows children in a school club noticing water and energy waste and taking practical steps to reduce it.

passage: My cousin Pooja is staying with us for the holidays, and my sister Mehak, who is nine, has turned into the house's light police. Pooja and I noticed it on the first day. Mehak walked behind Papa switching off the fan he'd left on. She put a bucket under the AC drip and used that water for the tulsi plant. When Pooja threw a half-full water bottle in the bin, Mehak fished it out, poured the water into the plant pot and said nothing. Pooja looked embarrassed. Later Mehak made a chart on the fridge with ticks for every switch turned off. I don't know if she learned it at school or just decided it herself. She won't say. 😅

qa.q: What did Mehak use the AC drip water for?
qa.a: She used it to water the tulsi plant.

qa.q: Why might Pooja have looked embarrassed?
qa.a: Mehak silently took out her half-full bottle and used the water, so Pooja probably realised she had wasted it and felt a little caught out.

qa.q: What could the family do to support Mehak's habits without making guests uncomfortable?
qa.a: They could join her fridge chart as a family game, so saving water and power feels shared rather than like someone checking on others.

qa.q: How might Papa see Mehak switching off the fan behind him?
qa.a: He might find it funny or a bit annoying at first, but it could also remind him to switch it off himself.

grounding: An older sibling describes a child building everyday habits to save water and electricity at home.

passage:
Week one: At the summer camp in Lisbon, Kishore's cabin threw away three bags of plastic cups in two days. Maria, their leader, held up one bag. "All this, in two days?" Kishore shrugged. Everyone did it.

Week two: Maria gave each camper a metal mug with a sticker for their name. Kishore lost his on the second day and had to ask for a paper cup. He hated being the only one. He found the mug under the bench and wrote his name again in marker.

Week three: The cabin bin held one small bag. Kishore reminded a younger boy, "Use your mug, not the cups," and felt a little proud of saying it.

qa.q: What did Maria give each camper in week two?
qa.a: She gave each camper a metal mug with a name sticker.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he had to ask for a paper cup?
qa.a: He hated being the only one using it, which shows he felt awkward and had started caring about fitting the new habit.

qa.q: What made the change work across the three weeks?
qa.a: Maria made the waste visible, gave an easy alternative, and let the habit grow until the campers reminded each other.

qa.q: What would change if Maria had only lectured the cabin about plastic?
qa.a: Without the mugs and seeing the bags, Kishore might have kept shrugging, since he had no simple way to change what everyone did.

grounding: It shows a child changing a wasteful habit over three weeks into a small waste-reducing routine.

passage: In Durban, Zanele's little brother Pablo had started crying whenever Gogo came to visit, because Gogo always let Zanele help in the kitchen but said Pablo was too small. On Sunday, Zanele saw his face crumple again as Gogo handed her the wooden spoon. For a second she wanted to keep it; stirring the stew was her special job. Then she knelt down. "Pablo, you can shell the peas. That's important too." Gogo raised an eyebrow, then nodded and showed Pablo how to press the pod with his thumb. He dropped half on the floor. At lunch, Gogo told the story of her own big sister, who once let her stir the pot and nearly burnt the house down.

qa.q: What job did Zanele give Pablo in the kitchen?
qa.a: She asked him to shell the peas.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when Gogo handed her the wooden spoon?
qa.a: She wanted to keep her special stirring job, but she also felt sorry for Pablo when she saw his face crumple, so she had mixed feelings.

qa.q: How could Gogo help both children feel valued on her visits?
qa.a: She could give each child a real task of their own and teach them different skills, so neither feels left out.

qa.q: What is it like for Pablo to be handed the peas?
qa.a: He probably feels included and proud to have an important job, even if he drops half of them. 🥺

grounding: It shows a child handling sibling rivalry by including a younger brother, while a grandparent teaches and shares her own sibling story.

passage: Damini was nine when her grandfather moved into the old-age home near her school. On Saturdays she went with her little sister Harsha to visit. The common room smelled of Dettol and tea. Harsha was six and kept running off to press the lift buttons. Damini felt her face burn; the nurses were watching. "Harsha, sit," she hissed. Dadu only laughed. "Let her. Come, Damini, help me with this crossword." He showed her how to count the letters and think of rhymes. When Harsha came back, bored, Damini gave her the pencil to fill the easy boxes. Dadu winked at Damini, as if she had done something very grown-up.

qa.q: What did Harsha keep running off to do?
qa.a: She kept running off to press the lift buttons.

qa.q: Why did Damini feel her face burn when Harsha ran around?
qa.a: She was embarrassed because the nurses were watching and she felt responsible for her little sister's behaviour.

qa.q: What worked in the way Damini handled Harsha by the end?
qa.a: Instead of only scolding, she gave Harsha a small task with the pencil, so her sister could join in with Dadu instead of running off.

qa.q: How might Dadu see his granddaughters' visits?
qa.a: He seems to enjoy them, laughing at Harsha's energy and using the crossword to teach Damini, so the visits likely brighten his week.

grounding: It shows a child caring for a younger sibling and learning from a grandparent during visits to a care home.

passage: I'm Francis, from next door. Sumit, who's eleven, has two little twin brothers, and I used to hear him shouting at them through the wall. Last summer his grandmother came from Kerala for three months. Every evening I'd see her on their porch teaching Sumit how to peel mangoes in one long strip. The twins would try to grab the knife, and she'd hand them the seeds to suck instead. Sumit started doing the same thing when she wasn't there. Once I saw him split his biscuit into three. I don't know what he felt, but the shouting got less. When his grandmother left, he stood at the gate for a long time after the taxi turned.

qa.q: What did Sumit's grandmother teach him on the porch?
qa.a: She taught him how to peel mangoes in one long strip.

qa.q: What does Sumit standing at the gate after the taxi left suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt sad to see his grandmother go and had grown close to her during her stay.

qa.q: What could Sumit's parents do to keep the change going after the grandmother left?
qa.a: They could notice and praise his patience with the twins, and help him keep in touch with his grandmother by phone.

qa.q: Why might the twins see Sumit differently after the summer?
qa.a: Since he now shares biscuits and shouts less, they may start seeing him as someone kind to turn to, not just a bossy big brother.

grounding: A neighbour observes a boy learning patience with younger siblings from his visiting grandmother.

passage:
Day one, three weeks before boards: Rajni made a timetable with every subject crammed in, but on the first evening she spent forty minutes answering messages. She went to bed feeling sick and behind.

Day ten: Her friend Tejas showed her his trick: phone in the kitchen, twenty-five minutes of work, five minutes of walking around. Rajni tried it with chemistry. It was hard to sit still for the first two blocks, and she almost went for her phone. By the fourth, she had finished a whole chapter of questions.

The morning of the exam: Her hands were cold. She breathed slowly, read all the questions first, and started with the ones she knew. She finished with ten minutes to check.

qa.q: Where did Tejas keep his phone while studying?
qa.a: He kept his phone in the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel after the first evening of her timetable?
qa.a: She felt sick and behind, since forty minutes of messages had eaten her study time and made her doubt her plan.

qa.q: Which part of Rajni's exam morning approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Reading all the questions first and starting with ones she knew calmed her nerves and saved time, so she had ten minutes left to check.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel seeing Rajni use his trick?
qa.a: He might feel glad and a bit proud that his simple method helped a friend, and it may make them study partners.

grounding: It shows a teen moving over weeks from a crammed, distracted plan to focused revision and a calm exam strategy.

passage: Beta, when your Sonali Didi was in Class 12, she panicked like you are now. I was her tuition teacher, remember? Lokesh, sit, listen. Two months before the exam she came to me with ten textbooks and cried that she could not finish. I asked her to close them all and write on one page what she already knew for each chapter. The page with the fewest lines, that was where she started. She read for one hour, then tested herself without the book. She hated it; she said it felt like failing all day. But her marks in the practice papers went up steadily. On exam day she told me, "Sir, I wasn't calm, but I knew what I knew." That is what I want for you too.

qa.q: What did Sonali write on one page for each chapter?
qa.a: She wrote what she already knew for each chapter.

qa.q: Why did Sonali hate testing herself without the book?
qa.a: It felt like failing all day, because it showed her the gaps in her memory, which was uncomfortable even though it helped.

qa.q: What could Lokesh try from Sonali's story when planning his own revision?
qa.a: He could list what he knows for each chapter, start with the weakest one, and test himself instead of just rereading.

qa.q: How does the teacher seem to see Lokesh's panic?
qa.a: He sees it as normal and familiar, like Sonali's, and hopes Lokesh can feel the same quiet confidence even if he is not calm.

grounding: An elder teacher tells a younger student how a past pupil planned revision and handled a high-stakes exam.

passage: Reena had one week until her maths exam, and the builders next door had started drilling. Her small flat had no quiet corner. Her little sister Nandini practised the harmonium in the evenings. Reena snapped at her twice and then felt awful. On Tuesday she changed the plan. She went to the library before school opened, when it was empty, and did her hardest topics then. After school, with the drilling at its worst, she did easy revision: formula cards on the balcony, earplugs from her father's toolbox. She asked Nandini to practise at seven instead of six. Nandini sulked but agreed. On Sunday night, Reena did a full paper under time. She got stuck on one question and moved on.

qa.q: When did Reena go to the library to study?
qa.a: She went before school opened, when it was empty.

qa.q: What did Reena feel after snapping at Nandini?
qa.a: She felt awful, which shows she knew the stress of the noise was making her unfair to her sister.

qa.q: What was wise about how Reena split her study time?
qa.a: She matched her hardest topics to the quiet morning and saved easy formula cards for the noisy afternoon, instead of fighting the noise.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini to move her practice time?
qa.a: She loses her usual time and sulks, but agreeing to seven shows she is willing to help her sister, even if it costs her something.

grounding: It shows a teen planning revision around noise and time pressure and practising a timed paper before the exam.

passage: The panchayat school in their village had its first inter-class debate: should the pond be fenced off? Wasim, fifteen, was against it. At home he practised in front of his mother, Sudha Ammi, who was sorting onions. "Fencing is bad because it's ugly," he began. Ammi raised an eyebrow. "Is that all?" He scowled and went back to his notebook. By evening he had asked the fishermen how many families used the pond and how many children had fallen in last year. He wrote both numbers down. "The other side will say safety," he said. "So I'll say: a fence with a gate, and a rope for rescue." Ammi nodded slowly. "Now that's an argument."

qa.q: Who did Wasim ask about how many families used the pond?
qa.a: He asked the fishermen.

qa.q: Why did Wasim scowl when Ammi asked, "Is that all?"
qa.a: He felt his first argument was being dismissed and was a bit stung, though he also seemed to realise it was weak.

qa.q: What made Wasim's final argument stronger?
qa.a: He gathered real numbers from the fishermen and prepared a fair answer to the safety point instead of just calling the fence ugly.

qa.q: How might a student on the other side see Wasim's fence-with-a-gate idea?
qa.a: They might respect it because it takes their safety worry seriously, which could make the debate feel less like a fight.

grounding: It shows a teen building an argument with evidence and answering the opposing side fairly for a village debate.

passage: Daniel and Freya were paired for the Year 10 debate in Dublin: "Homework should be banned." They had to argue for it, though Freya secretly liked homework. Daniel wanted to open with, "Everyone hates it." Freya shook her head. "That's not evidence. The other team will laugh." They spent Thursday lunch in the library finding a survey on sleep and a report on how much homework actually helped at their age. Freya wrote the other side's best points on sticky notes. "If they say practice matters, we agree, but say it can happen in class." On the day, Daniel's voice shook a little. When a question stumped him, Freya passed him a sticky note. They lost by one vote, but the judge praised their fair rebuttals.

qa.q: Where did Daniel and Freya spend Thursday lunch?
qa.a: They spent it in the library.

qa.q: What does Daniel's shaking voice suggest about how he felt on the day?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous speaking in front of people, even though they had prepared well.

qa.q: Why was writing the other side's points on sticky notes a smart move?
qa.a: It let them plan fair answers in advance, so when a question stumped Daniel, Freya could pass him a ready response.

qa.q: How might Freya feel arguing a side she doesn't personally agree with?
qa.a: She may find it strange at first, but it can help her understand both views and argue more fairly. 🤔

grounding: It shows teens building claims with evidence and preparing to answer counter-arguments fairly in a debate.

passage: The girls' hostel common room became a courtroom on Saturday nights. This week Dilnaz, sixteen, argued that phones should be allowed after lights-out. Usha, the senior monitor, argued against. Dilnaz talked fast. "We need them to call home!" Usha nodded calmly. "You can call home at eight. What's the real reason?" Dilnaz opened her mouth, then stopped. She knew the real reason was watching videos. She took a breath. "Okay. Fair point. But some girls have parents on night shifts. Eight doesn't work for them." The room went quiet. Usha paused. "That's true. Maybe a rule for them, not everyone." Dilnaz sat down, heart still thumping, feeling like she'd lost and won at the same time.

qa.q: What time did Usha say the girls could call home?
qa.a: She said they could call home at eight.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz feel like she had lost and won at the same time?
qa.a: She had to admit her first reason was weak, but her new point about parents on night shifts was strong enough to change Usha's view.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do before the next debate to feel less rushed?
qa.a: She could think through her real reasons and the other side's likely questions in advance, so she leads with her strongest evidence.

qa.q: How might Usha see Dilnaz after this debate?
qa.a: She probably respects her more, because Dilnaz admitted a weak point honestly and then raised a fair argument that Usha had to accept.

grounding: It shows a teen answering a counter-argument honestly and building a fairer claim in a hostel debate.

passage: Last month my cousin Farhan wanted to buy a cricket bat that the ad said was "used by 9 out of 10 top players." I'm Bhupen, fifteen, and I almost told him to go for it. Then I remembered our maths teacher saying to always ask: 9 out of which 10? I looked at the small print. They had asked ten players, and nine of them had tried it once. That's not the same as using it. Farhan was annoyed with me at first. "You ruin everything," he said. Honestly, I felt a bit smug, and then bad for being smug. He bought a cheaper bat. Later he admitted it was fine. I still check small print now, even on biscuit packets.

qa.q: What did the small print say about the ten players?
qa.a: It said they asked ten players, and nine of them had tried the bat once.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling after pointing out the small print?
qa.a: He felt a bit smug for being right, and then bad for being smug, especially since Farhan was annoyed.

qa.q: How could Bhupen share this kind of check without annoying people?
qa.a: He could ask the question together with Farhan, like "which ten?", so it feels like working it out as a team, not correcting him.

qa.q: How might Farhan see the whole episode now?
qa.a: He was annoyed at first, but since the cheaper bat was fine, he may now see the check as useful rather than spoiling his fun.

grounding: A teen looks back on reading a percentage claim carefully instead of being fooled by the numbers.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 9:
Rehana came to me upset after a friend told her that girls who skip breakfast get lower marks, "it's a study, 30% lower." Rehana hasn't been hungry in the mornings and was scared. I asked her to bring the article. Together we looked: the study was of a small group, and it said 30% of the breakfast-skippers had lower marks, not that their marks were 30% lower. Her friend Ganga had mixed them up. Rehana laughed a little and said, "So it's nothing?" I said numbers can still point to something worth noticing, like sleep and routine, and she could talk to her parents about her mornings. She left calmer. I'll check in next week.

qa.q: What did the study actually say about breakfast-skippers?
qa.a: It said 30% of the breakfast-skippers had lower marks, not that their marks were 30% lower.

qa.q: Why was Rehana scared after talking to Ganga?
qa.a: She hadn't been hungry in the mornings and believed the claim meant her marks would drop sharply, so the number felt like a threat.

qa.q: How did the counsellor handle the claim, and why did it help?
qa.a: She read the original article with Rehana and showed the mix-up, while still suggesting she talk to her parents, so Rehana neither panicked nor dismissed it.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had checked the article before telling Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana might have avoided a scare, and Ganga could have shared the real finding in a way that was useful rather than frightening.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen learning to read a percentage claim carefully instead of being frightened by misread numbers.

passage:
Thursday
Ujjwal's fantasy team "has a 70% chance of winning" according to his app thing, so he bet me a samosa. I said fine. 70% isn't 100% 😅
We lost the samosa bet... I mean HE lost. His team lost. He was furious and said the numbers were fake. I tried to explain that 70% means if the same match happened ten times, his team would win about seven. So losing once isn't the numbers lying. He didn't want to hear it. Kamal, the know-it-all, he said.
I get it though. When the number is big it feels like a promise. Maths sir would be proud of me today. Samosa tomorrow. 🙂

qa.q: What did Ujjwal bet Kamal?
qa.a: He bet Kamal a samosa.

qa.q: Why was Ujjwal furious when his team lost?
qa.a: He had treated the 70% chance like a promise, so the loss felt like the numbers had lied to him.

qa.q: How could Kamal explain probability to Ujjwal in a way he might accept?
qa.a: He could wait until Ujjwal is less upset, then use a simple example like tossing a coin or rolling a die many times to show chances, not certainties.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see Kamal's explanation right after losing?
qa.a: In that moment it probably felt like being lectured by a know-it-all rather than helped, because he was already upset.

grounding: A teen's diary shows understanding a probability claim correctly and not treating a high chance as a certainty.

passage: In Rania's class in Madrid, a boy announced that kids who drink energy drinks score better in football trials, because "all the best players on the team drink them." Javier nodded along. Rania didn't. At lunch she said, "Maybe the best players just train more and buy drinks with their pocket money. The drink isn't the reason." Javier looked annoyed. "The coach even said they help." "Did he show anything? Or just say it?" Rania asked. That evening Javier searched for proper studies and found none that tested it. He grudgingly texted her: "Ok, no proof 🙄 still tasty." Rania sent back a thumbs-up and a note to check with the coach about the claim.

qa.q: What did the boy claim about energy drinks?
qa.a: He claimed that kids who drink them score better in football trials because all the best players drink them.

qa.q: How can you tell Javier was reluctant to change his mind?
qa.a: He looked annoyed and pointed to the coach, and even his text admitting there was no proof sounded grudging.

qa.q: What did Rania do that others could copy when they hear a claim?
qa.a: She asked whether something else could explain the pattern and whether the coach showed evidence or only said it.

qa.q: How might the boy who made the claim feel if Rania questioned him in class?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed or defensive, so a calm question in private may have gone down better than calling him out.

grounding: It shows teens questioning a claim that confuses correlation with causation and relies on authority rather than evidence.

passage: In the physics lab, Swati's group had to test whether heavier balls roll down the ramp faster. Aparna, the topper, said, "Of course they do, my brother said so." Swati wasn't so sure. "Let's just time it." They rolled a steel ball and a marble five times each. The results were almost the same, and the small differences kept changing. Aparna frowned at the notebook. "Maybe we did it wrong." Swati suggested they try ten more times, and change who held the stopwatch. The results still matched. Aparna crossed out her prediction and wrote the real numbers. "My brother's going to argue," she said. Swati grinned. "Show him the notebook."

qa.q: How many times did they roll each ball at first?
qa.a: They rolled each ball five times.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she frowned at the notebook?
qa.a: She was uneasy and a bit reluctant, because the results went against what she had been sure of and what her brother had said.

qa.q: Why was repeating the test and changing the stopwatch holder a good idea?
qa.a: It checked whether the result was due to chance or one person's timing, so the conclusion rested on stronger evidence.

qa.q: How might Aparna's brother react to the notebook?
qa.a: He might argue at first, but the repeated measurements give Aparna evidence that is harder to dismiss than just his opinion.

grounding: It shows teens judging a claim by testing it rather than trusting who said it.

passage:
Dear Chinmay,
You forwarded me that message again, the one saying people who eat breakfast early live longer, "backed by doctors." I know you mean well. But I read the actual study. They only found early eaters tend to live longer. It didn't prove breakfast does it. Maybe early eaters sleep earlier, walk more, or just have calmer jobs. And "backed by doctors" didn't name a single doctor.
I'm not saying breakfast is bad. Eat it if you like it! I'm saying the message sounds more sure than the study is. If you're worried about health, ask your own doctor.
Also please stop forwarding stuff to the family group at 6 am. Nani's phone buzzes and wakes her up 😅
Your brother,
Omkar

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim?
qa.a: It claimed people who eat breakfast early live longer and said it was backed by doctors.

qa.q: What does Omkar's line "I know you mean well" show about his feelings?
qa.a: He wants to correct Chinmay without hurting him, showing care for his brother even while disagreeing.

qa.q: What made Omkar's reply to the message sensible?
qa.a: He read the actual study, pointed out other explanations, noticed no doctor was named, and suggested asking a real doctor instead of trusting forwards.

qa.q: If you were Chinmay, how might you feel reading this email?
qa.a: You might feel a little corrected, but the warm tone and the joke about Nani's phone would make it easier to accept. 🙂

grounding: A teen's email to his brother separates correlation from causation and questions a claim resting on vague authority.
